title: Evals for Agentic Engineering and Repo Augmentation

tldr.content: Agent evals are a distinct discipline — environment-interactive tasks graded on outcomes (not prose), scored for reliability (pass^k) and cost — and eval-driven development (evals define capabilities before you build; automated evals gate every agent change and model upgrade in CI) is now vendor-recommended practice. This repo already runs a serious eval stack for one subsystem (frozen 30-scenario corpus with dev/validation/held-out splits, Wilson CIs, hard safety gates, blinded double adjudication) plus judge-like pipelines in five skills — but no skill has its own golden suite, there is no eval-runner CLI, and nothing re-evals on model/tool upgrades. Recommendation: adopt eval-driven development repo-wide in three waves — W1 thin runner CLI + per-skill golden suites minted from the .agents corpus for judge-heavy skills; W2 outcome-graded end-to-end suites + judge calibration for the in-house challenger/judge; defer live-model execution, dashboards, and monitoring until W1/W2 show signal.

executiveSummary.content:
Question: how are evals used in agentic engineering practice, and how can they augment this repo? -> Triage (DEEP, hybrid) -> 5 parallel researchers (taxonomy | practice | local inventory | tooling | failure modes) -> synthesis -> adversarial challenge -> judge -> remediate -> verified finding.

```text
external methodology (T1,T2,T4,T5)  --\                        /--> challenger (disproof)
                                    --> synthesis (draft 30 claims) --> judge (4-dim rubric)
local repo inventory (T3)         --/                        \--> per-claim verify -> SAVED
```

Strongest evidence: (a) Anthropic engineering guidance explicitly prescribes eval-driven development, two-suite regression/capability gating in CI/CD on every agent change and model upgrade, and outcome-over-trajectory grading [R-anthropic-demystifying]; (b) the repo's own orchestration/config eval stack already implements the textbook pattern — frozen splits, small-sample statistics, hard safety gates, blinded adjudication [R-local-eval-corpus, R-local-slo] — but only for one subsystem [R-local-eval-trace]; (c) Anthropic's Agent Skills guide demands 3+ eval scenarios per skill and ships no runner, so skill authors need exactly the runner this repo could factor out [R-claude-skills-bp]. Headline caveats: benchmark decay and judge bias are quantified and real (contamination, position/verbosity/self-preference bias), the small-n doctrine bounds initial investment (20-50 real failure cases, pass rate is a product decision), and one flagged source was relocated (404) and is listed unverified.

keyFindings.content:
K1. supported: Agent evaluation is a recognized discipline distinct from chatbot evals — multi-step, tool-using agents in interactive environments, graded on task/environment outcomes, reliability across repeats (pass^k), and cost. [R-agent-eval-survey][R-tau-bench][R-agents-that-matter] -> D1

K2. supported: Eval-driven development is the vendor-recommended practice: define target capabilities as evals before building; run automated evals in CI/CD on every agent change AND every model upgrade; keep a near-100% regression suite plus a growing capability suite that graduates into it. [R-anthropic-demystifying][R-hamel-evals] -> D2

K3. supported: The small-n high-signal doctrine: start from 20-50 real failure cases and manual error analysis before infrastructure; pass-rate thresholds are product decisions, not a fixed 100%. [R-hamel-evals-faq][R-anthropic-demystifying][R-hamel-evals] -> D2, D6

K4. supported: LLM-as-judge works only with calibration: position, verbosity, and self-preference biases are quantified; mitigations (position swap, reference-guided judging, different-model judge, rubrics, statistical debiasing) are measurably effective; track judge-vs-human precision/recall, not raw agreement. [R-mtbench][R-claude-develop-tests][R-hamel-evals][R-alpacaeval-lc][R-self-recognition] -> D6

K5. supported: This repo already contains a textbook eval stack for the orchestration/config subsystem: deterministic runner with 16 fixtures wired to `make test-deterministic`; frozen-label corpus of 30 scenarios in dev(12)/validation(8)/held-out(10) splits; Wilson 95% CIs; hard gates (falseVerified==0, duplicateEffects==0); blinded double adjudication with Cohen's kappa. [R-local-eval-trace][R-local-eval-corpus][R-local-slo][R-local-runner] -> D3

K6. supported: Judge-like machinery already pervades the skills: csm-deep-research challenger + 4-dimension rubric judge (<0.7 fail); csm-review challenger disproof; csm-review-python doctrine rubric with typed findings; csm-make-tests mutation validation + approval ledgers; csm-orchestrate typed-receipt evidence gates; csm-autoresearch evaluator-owned scoring. [R-local-deep-research][R-local-review][R-local-review-python][R-local-make-tests][R-local-orchestrate][R-local-autoresearch] -> D3

K7. supported: The gaps are concentrated and enumerable: no per-skill scored eval suites (per-skill unit test suites exist; only orchestration/config has a scored corpus), no eval-runner CLI, no aggregate pass-rate reporting, no model/tool-version regression evals, no cross-version skill-output drift detection, no post-deployment monitoring. [R-local-eval-corpus][R-local-eval-trace] -> D4

K8. supported: Anthropic's Agent Skills authoring guide prescribes evaluation-first skill development (build 3+ eval scenarios before skill docs) and provides no built-in runner — "Users can create their own evaluation system" — demand the repo's existing csm-eval-corpus/1 pattern can satisfy. [R-claude-skills-bp] -> D5

K9. supported: Local-first tooling compatible with a git-only schema-driven repo exists: promptfoo (declarative asserts incl. JSON-Schema validation, GitHub Action before/after gating, fail thresholds), UK AISI Inspect (dataset/solver/scorer, JSON .eval logs, sandboxes), SWE-bench harness minting from own repos; hosted platforms (LangSmith, Braintrust, Weave) are optional, and OpenAI's Evals platform deprecation (read-only 2026-10-31) warns against vendor-locked eval formats. [R-promptfoo-intro][R-promptfoo-assertions][R-promptfoo-action][R-inspect][R-swebench-repo][R-openai-evals-guide] -> D5

K10. supported: Static benchmarks decay and lie without controls: contamination inflates SWE-bench Verified scores; Arena-style private testing distorts leaderboards; harness/infra noise alone swung Terminal-Bench 2.0 by 6 points (distrust <3-point gaps); mitigations are fresh task streams, documented eval configuration, and reliability+cost reporting. [R-swe-rebench][R-arena-private][R-anthropic-infra-noise][R-swebench-live] -> D6

K11. partially-supported: Highest-leverage repo changes: W1 — factor the existing runner/corpus pattern into a thin eval CLI and mint per-skill golden suites from the .agents corpus (~34 findings, 48 plans, 9 reviews; requires triage), starting with judge-heavy skills that emit typed JSON; W2 — outcome-graded end-to-end suites and judge-calibration for the in-house challenger/judge; W3 — defer live-model execution, dashboards, monitoring. [R-local-eval-corpus][R-anthropic-demystifying][R-hamel-evals-faq] -> D7

detailSections.content:
D1. What agent evals are (expands K1)
One-line: agents are evaluated on what they did in an environment, not what they said.
Surveys now treat agent evaluation as its own field across five perspectives [R-agent-eval-survey]. AgentBench runs LLMs as agents across 8 interactive environments [R-agentbench]; GAIA pits models against tool/multimodal questions trivial for humans (92% vs 15% GPT-4+plugins) [R-gaia]; WebArena scores functional correctness on self-hosted sites (GPT-4 14.41% vs human 78.24%) [R-webarena]; OSWorld uses per-task execution scripts in real OSes [R-osworld]; tau-bench grades the final database state against an annotated goal state and introduced pass^k for consistency across repeats (gpt-4o retail pass^8 <25%) [R-tau-bench]; SWE-bench resolves real GitHub issues verified by fail-to-pass tests [R-swebench]. 'AI Agents That Matter' adds the cost axis: accuracy-only optimization produces needlessly costly agents [R-agents-that-matter]. METR's time-horizon methodology shows the right yardstick is task length at fixed reliability (50% horizon doubling ~7 months) [R-metr].

D2. Agentic engineering practice (expands K2, K3)
One-line: write evals first, gate every change, mine production failures, grade outcomes.
Anthropic recommends eval-driven development — "build evals to define planned capabilities before agents can fulfill them" — with automated evals in CI/CD as first line of defense on each agent change and model upgrade, a near-100% regression suite, and capability evals that graduate into it [R-anthropic-demystifying]. Claude Code itself moved to dedicated evals (concision, file edits, over-engineering) as it scaled. Task sourcing: mine bug trackers and support queues; start with 20-50 real failures [R-anthropic-demystifying][R-hamel-evals-faq]. Contradiction ledger: Anthropic prescribes eval-first development, while Hamel Husain's evals FAQ answers "Should I practice eval-driven development? Generally no" — the error-analysis-first school (manually review 20-50 real outputs before writing any tests) [R-hamel-evals-faq]. Resolution adopted in this finding: both schools demand durable eval suites; they differ on ordering and cost bounds. The repo's structure (typed skill outputs, existing corpus/runner pattern) makes Anthropic's eval-first order cheap to follow for skill authoring, and Hamel's small-n bounds (20-50 cases per suite, pass rate as a product decision) cap the investment regardless of ordering [R-hamel-evals-faq][R-hamel-evals]. Hamel's ladder — Level 1 asserts on every change, Level 2 model/human eval on cadence, Level 3 A/B after significant change — with pass rate as a product decision [R-hamel-evals]; Rechat ran hundreds of LLM unit tests in standard CI [R-hamel-evals]. The harness is itself the variable: SWE-agent's interface functions alone hit then-SOTA 12.5% [R-swe-agent]; SWE-bench scores vary significantly with scaffolding at fixed model [R-anthropic-swebench]; Aider's leaderboard fixes the harness and reports pass1/pass2 + cost [R-aider]. Standing harnesses catch silent model-upgrade regressions (Voiceflow: -10% intent accuracy caught on a silent gpt-3.5 swap; practitioner-reported) [R-yan].

D3. What this repo already has (expands K5, K6)
One-line: the textbook pattern exists — for one subsystem — plus judge pipelines inside five skills.
```text
frozen corpus (30 scenarios; dev 12 / val 8 / held-out 10; labelsFrozen)
   -> deterministic runner (tests/evals/runner.mjs, 16 fixtures, make test-deterministic)
   -> SLI/SLO metrics + Wilson 95% CI (INSUFFICIENT_DATA, never silent 0)
   -> hard safety gates: falseVerified==0, duplicateEffects==0 (fault-injection tested)
   -> blinded double adjudication (hidden verdicts, pairwise agreement + Cohen's kappa)
```
Evidence: [R-local-eval-trace][R-local-eval-corpus][R-local-slo][R-local-runner][R-local-safety-gate]. Precision note: the 16-fixture runner is wired to `make test-deterministic`; the 30-scenario corpus executes as node --test suites under tests/evals/orchestration/ and is not reachable via any make target. Judge-like machinery: csm-deep-research's challenger (uphold/downgrade/retract/suggest_new_claim) + judge scoring factual/citation accuracy, completeness, clarity 0-1 with <0.7 fail and reasoning-before-verdict [R-local-deep-research]; csm-review's independent challenger disproof of every C/H/M finding [R-local-review]; csm-review-python's fixed doctrine rubric emitting typed findings JSON [R-local-review-python]; csm-make-tests' mutation kill-scores as the protection metric in append-only approval ledgers [R-local-make-tests]; csm-orchestrate's typed receipts and technical/functional/adversarial/final gates [R-local-orchestrate]; csm-autoresearch's evaluator-owned hill-climbing with hard gates where candidates never own their score [R-local-autoresearch]. The schema registry is immutable, digest-pinned, and rejects unknown revisions — machine-checkable eval observations [R-local-registry].

D4. Gap analysis (expands K7)
One-line: one subsystem is evaluated; the skills themselves — the repo's actual product — are not.
The only scored corpus targets orchestration/config assurance; glob of tests/evals/** finds no corpus for csm-plan, csm-grill, csm-review, csm-deep-research, csm-build, or any other skill [R-local-eval-corpus]. No eval-runner CLI exists (scripts/ holds 13 utilities, none eval-running; evals execute only as node --test suites) [R-local-eval-trace]. No model/tool-version regression evals (zero hits for model-version in tests/), no aggregate pass-rate dashboards, no post-deployment monitoring — the repo's own docs mark monitoring "none yet" and defer live model execution [R-local-eval-corpus]. Labeled failure cases exist only as fault-injection scenarios at the harness level [R-local-safety-gate]. The raw material for minting suites exists and is substantial: .agents/ holds ~34 dated research findings, 48 plans, and 9 typed reviews, though it mixes formats and includes exploratory outputs, so minting requires triage [R-local-make-tests].

D5. Tooling fit and the skills-eval niche (expands K8, K9)
One-line: build on in-repo formats; borrow patterns (not lock-in) from promptfoo/Inspect; the skill-eval runner niche is unfilled by vendors.
promptfoo runs entirely locally with declarative YAML asserts spanning equals/contains/regex/javascript/is-json + JSON-Schema validation and llm-rubric [R-promptfoo-intro][R-promptfoo-assertions]; its GitHub Action gates PRs with before/after comparisons [R-promptfoo-action] and CI can fail builds on thresholds [R-promptfoo-cicd]. Inspect composes Dataset+Solver+Scorer with sandboxed execution and writes JSON .eval logs — eval results as committed, diffable artifacts [R-inspect][R-inspect-logs]. SWE-bench's collection procedure can mint private tasks from your own repositories [R-swebench-repo]. Hosted options exist (LangSmith versioned datasets for CI pinning [R-langsmith]; Braintrust eval-action with reporter-controlled exit codes and smoke modes [R-braintrust]; W&B Weave versioned dataset objects [R-weave]) but require accounts/API keys [R-weave]. Vendor churn is real: OpenAI's Evals platform goes read-only 2026-10-31 [R-openai-evals-guide]. Most telling: Anthropic's own skill-authoring guide mandates 3+ eval scenarios per skill with a JSON fixture of query/files/expected_behavior, then states there is no built-in runner — users must build their own [R-claude-skills-bp]; its frontmatter constraints (name <=64 lowercase-hyphen, description <=1024) are a cheap deterministic pre-LLM gate [R-claude-skills-bp]. The repo's csm-eval-corpus/1 + runner + SLO gate pattern is exactly that missing runner, already schema-typed.

D6. Failure modes, economics, governance (expands K3, K4, K10)
One-line: evals mislead via decay and biased judges; calibrate, keep them fresh, and pay for judges only where asserts cannot reach.
Decay: contamination inflates some SWE-bench Verified scores; continuous decontaminated streams (SWE-rebench, 21k+ tasks) and live benchmarks (SWE-bench-Live, 1,319 post-2024 tasks) are the countermeasures [R-swe-rebench][R-swebench-live]. Gaming: undisclosed private testing on Arena (27 private Meta variants pre-Llama-4) with up to 112% relative gains from extra arena-distribution data [R-arena-private]. Noise: infra resourcing alone swung Terminal-Bench 2.0 by 6 points; distrust <3-point gaps unless configuration is matched [R-anthropic-infra-noise]. Judge bias: position (Claude-v1 favored first position 75% of cases, 23.8% swap-consistency), verbosity (repetitive-list attack defeated Claude-v1/GPT-3.5 91.3% of the time), self-preference linearly correlated with self-recognition [R-mtbench][R-self-recognition]; mitigations measured — position swap + reference-guided judging cut GPT-4 math-grading failures 70%->15%; length-controlled AlpacaEval raised human-rank correlation 0.94->0.98 [R-mtbench][R-alpacaeval-lc]; Anthropic directs using a different model to judge than to generate [R-claude-develop-tests] (Hamel's FAQ dissents on the default: judge-human alignment on a held-out labeled set is what matters, and he does not advocate a different judge model unless alignment fails [R-hamel-evals-faq]). Calibrate judges to named humans on 25-50-example batches with precision/recall, never raw agreement on imbalanced data [R-hamel-evals]. Economics: strong teams spend 60-80% of dev time on error analysis/evals; asserts are near-free, judges are expensive — reserve them for persistent high-value failure modes [R-hamel-evals-faq]. Governance exemplars: golden-answer sign-off apps, geo confinement, abuse-monitoring opt-out, no training on judge outputs [R-databricks]. Evals are experiments: report CIs and plan sample sizes [R-error-bars].

D7. Change options for this repo (expands K11)
One-line: extend a proven in-repo pattern outward — runner, suites, calibration — before buying anything hosted.
```text
W1 (do now):  thin `eval` CLI over tests/evals runner pattern
              + per-skill csm-eval-corpus/1 suites (start 20-50 cases each)
              + mint cases from .agents corpus (~34 findings / 48 plans / 9 reviews; triage first)
              + Makefile gate: pass-rate threshold = product decision; hard gates absolute
              first skills: csm-review, csm-deep-research (typed JSON outputs = cheap deterministic scoring)
W2 (pilot):   outcome-graded end-to-end task suites (tau-bench-style: grade final artifact state)
              + judge calibration: challenger/judge verdicts vs human adjudication (precision/recall)
              + re-eval trigger on model/tool version changes (registry-pinned versions)
W3 (defer):   live-model execution, dashboards, post-deployment monitoring
Avoid:        hosted lock-in for core formats; exact-trajectory gating (brittle); 100% pass-rate dogma;
              chasing public benchmarks; judge-everything (asserts first)
```
Conditions/measures: W1 needs only existing machinery (corpus schema, runner, Wilson gates) [R-local-eval-corpus][R-local-slo]; success measure = regression suite catches a seeded defect and a real regression before merge; W2 success measure = judge-human precision/recall reported per dimension with CIs [R-hamel-evals]; rollback = suites are additive files under tests/evals/, removable without touching skills. What would change this: if promptfoo's YAML ergonomics prove cheaper than extending csm-eval-corpus/1, adopt promptfoo as the runner and keep the corpus format as source of truth [R-promptfoo-intro].

recommendation.content:
Adopt eval-driven development for the skills themselves, built on the repo's existing eval pattern rather than new tooling. Confidence: high for W1 (all components exist in-repo and the practice is vendor-recommended [R-anthropic-demystifying][R-local-eval-corpus]); medium for W2 (judge calibration is evidenced but its cost is real [R-hamel-evals-faq]); W3 deferred.

Do now (W1): (1) factor tests/evals/runner.mjs into a thin eval-runner CLI with the corpus manifest as input; (2) mint per-skill golden suites of 20-50 real cases from the .agents corpus (triage first — it mixes formats and exploratory outputs), starting with csm-review and csm-deep-research because their typed JSON verdicts score deterministically without a judge; (3) wire a Makefile gate — pass-rate threshold set as an explicit product decision, hard safety gates absolute (the falseVerified==0 pattern) [R-local-slo][R-hamel-evals].

Pilot next (W2): outcome-graded end-to-end suites (grade the produced artifact/state, not the trajectory [R-anthropic-demystifying][R-tau-bench]); calibrate the in-house challenger/judge against human adjudication with precision/recall on 25-50-example batches [R-hamel-evals]; add re-eval triggers on model and tool version changes pinned via the schema registry [R-local-registry][R-yan].

Defer (W3) live-model execution, dashboards, and monitoring until W1/W2 demonstrate catches; prefer promptfoo/Inspect patterns over adoption unless authoring ergonomics beat the in-repo format, and avoid hosted-only formats (OpenAI Evals deprecation shows the churn risk [R-openai-evals-guide]).

Cost of being wrong: over-investment is bounded by the small-n doctrine (stop at 20-50 cases/skill until a real regression is caught or missed); under-investment risks silent regressions on model upgrades, which are documented and reach 10% task-level drops [R-yan]. What would change the recommendation: evidence that .agents corpus cases cannot be converted to deterministic cases at reasonable cost would push W1 toward promptfoo-style rubric asserts instead.

processAppendix.content:
Tier: DEEP. Source mode: hybrid. Clarifications: OFF (recorded assumptions). Tmux session: csm-deep-research-agentic-evals.

Tracks and returns: T1 eval taxonomy (web, 16 claims); T2 agentic engineering practice (web, 16); T3 local repo inventory (local, 16); T4 tooling and integration (web, 16); T5 failure modes/economics/governance (web, 16). All 5 researchers returned; no resilience rungs consumed.

Browser retrieval fallback: 1 flagged URL (anthropic.com/engineering/developing-an-effective-evals-suite) retrieved by primary via csm-browse (sid=research-agentic-evals) — rendered 404 (post relocated); session closed 2026-08-29T09:19Z; claim left unverified. T2's openai.com SWE-bench-Verified 403 was covered by a secondary source and is cited as such.

Local-source convention: T3 file:// locators mirrored as GitHub blob URLs at origin/main (verified via git cat-file on all 13 cited files); publisher marked workspace-local.

Assumptions recorded: (a) 'evals' read as evaluation suites for agents/skills, including benchmarks where they inform practice; (b) the repo's product = the skills and their assurance machinery; (c) OpenAI deprecation banner taken at face value and listed unverified.

Challenger verdicts (independent, anti-anchored; 30 claims): uphold — claims 1-12, 14, 17, 19-24, 26-29 (24 total; all citations re-located and quotes verified, including local file reads for claims 5, 6, 7, 24, 26 and live-page re-fetches for claims 2, 8, 9, 10, 20, 22, 23, 28). downgrade — claim-13 (single 10% case, deprecation-driven upgrade not 'silent'; secondary source), claim-15 (cost-reporting mis-attributed to Error-Bars paper), claim-16 (70%->15% is reference-guided alone), claim-18 (METR page flags doubling-time as superseded by TH 1.1), claim-25 (counts: 34 findings not 33; corpus mixes formats, needs triage). claim-30 upheld as labeled synthesis with scope notes (triage caveat; judge-heavy start is a design choice). Cross-cutting: (1) doctrine conflict Anthropic eval-first vs Hamel error-analysis-first — surfaced with a contradiction ledger in D2; (2) precision notes applied (corpus not on a make target; scored suites vs unit suites; typed-receipt citation widened). Challenger output truncated at cross-cutting item 2; residual items unrecorded (process note).

Remediation log (applied by primary): claim-13 rewritten (statement, verdict partially-supported retained); claim-15 rewritten + added ref-agents-that-matter citation; claim-16 corrected; claim-18 supersession note added; claim-25/K11/D4/recommendation counts corrected to ~34 + triage note; claim-30 scope notes added; K7 clarified (scored vs unit suites); D2 contradiction ledger added; D3 precision note added. All edits re-verified against the challenger's proposed wordings.

Judge scores: factual accuracy 0.9, citation accuracy 0.9, completeness 0.95, clarity 0.9 — PASS (independent judge; reasoning-before-verdict; spot-checked load-bearing claims and re-counted corpus 34/48/9). Two non-blocking follow-ups were applied at REMEDIATE (D7 count fix; deprecation-banner quote). VERIFY scale: DEEP per-claim (verdicts recorded in claims array). Journal: see journal array (live Control journal).

claims.statement: Agent evaluation is a recognized discipline distinct from chatbot evals: multi-step tool-using agents in interactive environments, graded on task/environment outcomes, reliability across repeats (pass^k), and cost.

citations.quote: This paper provides the first comprehensive survey of evaluation methods for these increasingly capable agents.
a benchmark emulating dynamic conversations between a user (simulated by language models) and a language agent provided with domain-specific API tools and policy guidelines
First, there is a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly

claims.statement: Anthropic recommends eval-driven development: define target capabilities as evals before agents can fulfill them; run automated evals in CI/CD on every agent change and every model upgrade; maintain a near-100% regression suite plus capability evals that graduate into it.

citations.quote: We recommend practicing eval-driven development: build evals to define planned capabilities before agents can fulfill them, then iterate until the agent performs well.
Automated evals are especially useful pre-launch and in CI/CD, running on each agent change and model upgrade as the first line of defense against quality problems.
Regression evals ask, "Does the agent still handle all the tasks it used to?" and should have a nearly 100% pass rate.

claims.statement: Practitioner consensus prescribes starting evals from 20-50 real failure cases with manual error analysis before building infrastructure; pass-rate thresholds are product decisions, not a fixed 100%.

citations.quote: Spend 30 minutes manually reviewing 20-50 LLM outputs whenever you make significant changes.
Converting user-reported failures into test cases ensures your suite reflects actual usage; prioritizing by user impact helps you invest effort where it counts.
unlike traditional unit tests, you don't necessarily need a 100% pass rate. Your pass rate is a product decision, depending on the failures you are willing to tolerate.

claims.statement: LLM-as-judge exhibits quantified position, verbosity, and self-preference biases; mitigations (position swap, reference-guided judging, different-model judge, statistical debiasing) are measurably effective; judges must be calibrated against human labels using precision/recall rather than raw agreement.

citations.quote: We examine the usage and limitations of LLM-as-a-judge, including position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, as well as limited reasoning ability, and propose solutions to mitigate some of them.
Generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate than the model used to generate the evaluated output
using raw agreement is generally not recommended and can be misleading when classes are imbalanced. Instead, you should typically measure precision and recall separately

Proportions carry a **Wilson 95% confidence interval** (z = 1.959963984540054, correct small-sample coverage including the 0/1 boundaries). Empty populations report `INSUFFICIENT_DATA`, never a silent 0.

citations.quote: The rubric is stable and explicit: factual accuracy … citation accuracy … completeness … and clarity … Each dimension is scored 0-1 — a dimension fails at < 0.7
The challenger attempts disproof: re-locate the citation; check reachability/exploitability against actual call sites; look for mitigations the finder missed; check anchor applicability.
Record per-module mutation scores in the ledger — this, not coverage percentage, is the protection metric.

claims.statement: The repo lacks: per-skill golden task suites (only the orchestration/config stack is scored), an eval-runner CLI, aggregate pass-rate reporting, model/tool-version regression evals, cross-version skill-output drift detection, and post-deployment monitoring.

citations.quote: Live model execution, telemetry, dashboards, provider calls, and A2A are intentionally outside this gate.
Corpora are separate JSON manifests under `tests/evals/orchestration/corpus/`, each declared as `csm-eval-corpus/1`

claims.statement: Anthropic's Agent Skills authoring guide prescribes evaluation-first skill development (build 3+ eval scenarios before skill docs) and provides no built-in runner, telling users to create their own evaluation system.

citations.quote: There is not currently a built-in way to run these evaluations. Users can create their own evaluation system.

claims.statement: Mature local-first eval tooling compatible with a git-only schema-driven repo exists: promptfoo (local execution, declarative asserts including JSON-Schema validation, GitHub Action before/after gating, CI fail thresholds), UK AISI Inspect (dataset/solver/scorer composition, sandboxed execution, JSON .eval logs), and SWE-bench harness procedures for minting private tasks from own repositories.

citations.quote: Private: This software runs completely locally. The evals run on your machine and talk directly with the LLM.
Different types of assertions can be used to validate the output in various ways, such as checking for equality, JSON structure, similarity, or custom functions.
Inspect log files use JSON to represent the hierarchy of data produced by an evaluation.
Run SWE-bench's data collection procedure on your own repositories, to make new SWE-Bench tasks.

claims.statement: Static benchmarks decay and mislead without controls: contamination inflates some SWE-bench Verified scores; undisclosed private leaderboard testing distorts rankings; harness/infra configuration alone swung Terminal-Bench 2.0 scores by 6 percentage points; mitigations include continuously refreshed task streams, documented eval configuration, and joint accuracy-cost reporting.

citations.quote: show that performance of some language models might be inflated due to contamination issues
At an extreme, we identify 27 private Llama-4 variants tested by Meta
In internal experiments, the gap between the most- and least-resourced setups on Terminal-Bench 2.0 was 6 percentage points (p < 0.01).

claims.statement: Agent evals should grade outcomes rather than exact tool-call trajectories: exact-sequence checks are brittle; tau-bench grades final database state against an annotated goal state; pass^k measures reliability across repeated runs.

citations.quote: it's often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took.
even state-of-the-art function calling agents (like gpt-4o) succeed on <50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent (pass^8 <25% in retail)

claims.statement: The agent harness is a first-class eval variable: SWE-agent's purpose-built agent-computer interface alone reached then-SOTA 12.5% pass@1 on SWE-bench; SWE-bench performance varies significantly with scaffolding at fixed underlying model; Aider's leaderboard fixes the harness to compare models, reporting first/second-attempt pass rates and cost.

citations.quote: SWE-agent's custom agent-computer interface (ACI) significantly enhances an agent's ability to create and edit code files, navigate entire repositories, and execute tests and other programs.
The performance of an agent on SWE-bench can vary significantly based on this scaffolding, even when using the same underlying AI model.

claims.statement: A documented model-version upgrade (gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 to gpt-3.5-turbo-1106) caused a 10% intent-classification regression that Voiceflow's standing eval harness caught (practitioner-reported, secondary source; primary blog 404); Anthropic prescribes model upgrades as a first-class CI/CD eval trigger.

citations.quote: Voiceflow's eval harness for intent classification helped them catch a 10% performance drop when upgrading from the deprecating gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 to the more recent gpt-3.5-turbo-1106.
running on each agent change and model upgrade as the first line of defense against quality problems

claims.statement: Strong teams spend 60-80% of development time on error analysis and evaluation; assertions are near-free while LLM-judge evaluators carry heavy ongoing cost, so judges are reserved for persistent high-value failure modes; Level-1 asserts run on every change.

citations.quote: we've spent 60-80% of our development time on error analysis and evaluation.
I often run Level 1 evals on every code change, Level 2 on a set cadence and Level 3 only after significant product changes.

claims.statement: Evals are experiments subject to sampling noise: confidence intervals on scores and differences plus sample-size planning are the prescribed statistical practice (Adding Error Bars to Evals); joint accuracy-cost reporting is the separate prescription of AI Agents That Matter.

citations.quote: Fundamentally, evaluations are experiments; but the literature on evaluations has largely ignored the literature from other sciences on experiment analysis and planning.
a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly

claims.statement: Judge-bias magnitudes are quantified: on near-identical pairs Claude-v1 favored the first position 75% of the time with 23.8% swap-consistency; a repetitive-list verbosity attack defeated Claude-v1/GPT-3.5 judges 91.3% of the time; answer reordering alone made Vicuna-13B 'beat' ChatGPT on 66/80 queries; reference-guided grading alone cut GPT-4 math-grading failure from 70% to 15% (position-swap is a separate mitigation for position bias).

citations.quote: The position bias can be very significant. Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases.
Vicuna-13B could beat ChatGPT on 66 over 80 tested queries with ChatGPT as an evaluator.

claims.statement: Statistical debiasing of judges works: length-controlled AlpacaEval improves robustness to verbosity manipulation and raised Spearman correlation with human Arena rankings from 0.94 to 0.98; self-preference is linearly correlated with self-recognition capability.

citations.quote: increases the Spearman correlation with LMSYS Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.
we discover a linear correlation between self-recognition capability and the strength of self-preference bias.

claims.statement: METR's methodology measures task length (expert human time) an agent completes at 50% reliability, finding the horizon doubling roughly every 7 months across six years (original March 2025 analysis; the page flags the doubling-time claim as superseded by updated Time Horizon 1.1 figures) — an exemplar of reliability-conditioned capability metrics.

citations.quote: The length of tasks (measured by how long they take human professionals) that generalist frontier model agents can complete autonomously with 50% reliability has been doubling approximately every 7 months for the last 6 years.

claims.statement: Terminal-Bench 2.0 is a curated benchmark of 89 hard terminal-environment tasks, each with a unique environment, human-written reference solution, and verification tests; frontier models scored under 65% at publication.

citations.quote: a carefully curated hard benchmark composed of 89 tasks in computer terminal environments inspired by problems from real workflows.

claims.statement: OpenAI's Evals platform is being deprecated (read-only 2026-10-31, shutdown 2026-11-30), steering users to Datasets — evidence of eval-tooling vendor churn and an argument for in-repo formats.

citations.locator: deprecation banner, fetched 2026-08-29 (quote re-verified by challenger)
citations.quote: Evals will become read-only for existing users on October 31, 2026, and the platform is scheduled to shut down on November 30, 2026

claims.statement: Hosted eval platforms provide CI integration patterns — LangSmith versioned datasets for CI pinning; Braintrust GitHub Action and bt eval with reporter-controlled exit codes and smoke modes; W&B Weave versioned dataset objects — but require hosted accounts/API keys.

citations.quote: Offline evaluations target examples from datasets: curated test cases with reference outputs that define what 'good' looks like.
Integrate evaluations into your CI/CD pipeline to catch regressions before they reach production.
A Dataset is a collection of examples stored as a Weave object. Publishing the dataset to Weave versions it and makes it reusable across evaluation runs.

claims.statement: Anthropic's eval-building guidance prioritizes volume of automatically graded questions over few hand-graded ones, and recommends structuring questions for automated grading (multiple-choice, string match, code-graded, LLM-graded).

citations.quote: Prioritize volume over quality: More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals.

claims.statement: SKILL.md frontmatter constraints (name <=64 chars lowercase/numbers/hyphens; description <=1024 chars, non-empty, no XML tags) are machine-checkable, making frontmatter schema validation a cheap deterministic pre-LLM eval gate.

citations.quote: name: Maximum 64 characters, lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens only, no XML tags, no reserved words

claims.statement: The repo's schemas/registry.json is an immutable, digest-pinned schema registry with reject-on-unknown-revision policy — machine-checkable eval observations.

citations.quote: assert.equal(laxResult.falseVerified, true); assert.equal(laxResult.details.injectedFault, "lax-provenance-verifier");

claims.statement: Off-the-shelf/generic evals routinely fail for real applications because they barely correlate with application-specific performance; application/task-specific evals are required.

citations.quote: They barely correlate with application-specific performance and aren't discriminative enough to use in production.

claims.statement: Enterprise eval governance ships as product controls: human review apps for golden-answer sign-off, geo-confinement of judge processing, abuse-monitoring opt-outs so eval data is not retained by judge providers, and prohibitions on training models on judge outputs.

citations.quote: For Azure OpenAI, Databricks has opted out of Abuse Monitoring so no prompts or responses are stored with Azure OpenAI.

claims.statement: UK AISI Inspect includes a sandboxing system for running untrusted model-generated code during agent evals (Docker, Kubernetes, Modal, and others via an extension API).

citations.quote: A sandboxing system that supports running untrusted model code in Docker, Kubernetes, Modal, Proxmox, Vagrant, and other systems via an extension API.
